source: Standard Candles
Cepheid variables and type Ia supernovae have known luminosities, so how bright they look tells how far away they are.
Students think every star of the same brightness in the sky is at the same distance.

Parallax works only for nearby stars. To reach other galaxies, astronomers use standard candles: objects whose luminosity $L$ is known. Measure how bright one looks, $b$, and the inverse-square law gives its distance: $d = \sqrt{\dfrac{L}{4\pi b}}$.

The hard part is knowing $L$. Cepheid variables are pulsating yellow supergiant stars that brighten and dim every few days to a few months. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt, studying Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud (all about the same distance from us), found that the longer a Cepheid's period, the more luminous it is. So timing a Cepheid tells its luminosity, and its brightness then tells its distance. Cepheids are bright enough to see in galaxies tens of millions of light-years away. For greater distances, astronomers use type Ia supernovae, exploding white dwarfs that blow up at nearly the same mass and so peak at nearly the same luminosity, about 5 billion Suns, visible billions of light-years away. Each rung is calibrated by the one below: parallax fixes the nearest Cepheids, Cepheids fix the supernovae.

A standard candle has a known luminosity, so its apparent brightness gives its distance: for two of the same kind, $\dfrac{d_2}{d_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}}$. Cepheids (period tells luminosity) and type Ia supernovae (nearly equal peaks) are the main ones.
A Cepheid's brightness rising and falling, and the period–luminosity relation: from the period, read the luminosity (absolute magnitude).
Worked examples
A 10-day Cepheid in our galaxy is $1000$ pc away. A 10-day Cepheid in another galaxy looks $10^{8}$ times fainter. How far is that galaxy?
Two Cepheids
Same period, same luminosity, so $\frac{d_2}{d_1} = \sqrt{\frac{b_1}{b_2}} = \sqrt{10^{8}} = 10^{4}$.
$d_2 = 10^{4} \times 1000 = 10^{7}$ pc $= 10$ Mpc, about 33 million light-years.
A type Ia supernova in a galaxy $20$ Mpc away peaked $400$ times brighter than one in a distant galaxy. How far is the distant one?
Supernovae
$d_2 = 20 \times 20 = 400$ Mpc, about 1.3 billion light-years.

Two stars that look equally bright are not necessarily equally far away: one might be a dim star nearby, the other a brilliant star far off. Brightness alone tells nothing about distance unless you know the luminosity. Check: Procyon and Rigel look about equally bright, yet Rigel is about 75 times farther away, so by the inverse-square law it must be thousands of times more luminous.
The cosmic distance ladder: each method covers a range of distances and is calibrated by the one below it.
